Notes: Earliest documented Jewish presence (Year Established c. 20 CE): Josephus, Antiquities 18.9.1 (18.311-313), in the narrative of Asinaeus and Anilaeus under the Parthian king Artabanus III (their 'state' c. 18-33 CE), states that Nisibis, like Nehardea, served the Jews of Babylonia as a treasury where they deposited the half-shekel and other votive offerings for the Jerusalem Temple, later carried to Jerusalem by 'many ten thousand men' for fear of Parthian robbers. Date c. 20 CE (narrative setting; the custom itself is undated). Indicates a resident organized Jewish community. The tens of thousands of escorts are a convoy/pilgrim figure for Babylonian Jewry as a whole, not Nisibis residents, so Population blank. Pre-Josephus claims (Assyrian deportees of 722 BCE on the Habor near Nusaybin, per a Turkish article not accessed) are tradition, not documented presence at Nisibis.

Event: after Izates of Adiabene (a convert to Judaism; ruled 36-60 CE) helped restore Artabanus III to the Parthian throne (Artabanus returned in 36), 'the city of Nisibis was added to his dominions' (Jewish Encyclopedia, Adiabene; cf. Josephus, Antiquities 20.3.3 / 20.68). Nisibis thus came under a Judaizing royal house c. 36 CE. Political event; not itself a count of Jewish residents.

Event, c. 40 CE (Josephus, Antiquities 18.9.9 / 18.379): Jews of Babylonia who had fled to Seleucia after the fall of Anilaeus (c. 35) and were attacked there (over 50000 said slain in Seleucia - a death toll in Seleucia, not Nisibis) fled to Ctesiphon and then to Nehardea and Nisibis, finding security in the strength of those cities. Encyclopaedia Judaica (Ashtor and Beer): 'The community appears to have been well founded because it also absorbed the Jews of Seleucia and Ctesiphon.' Date c. 40: five-six years after the arrival in Seleucia c. 35. No numbers for Nisibis.

Scholarly assessment (Jewish Encyclopedia, 'Bathyra'): R. Judah b. Bathyra (I) 'must have lived before the destruction of the Temple' and 'At Nisibis in Mesopotamia he had a famous college'. Dated to mid-1st c. CE (midpoint 50; c.). A rabbinic school implies an established, learned community; no size given.

Babylonian Talmud Pesachim 3b (baraita-type story set while the Temple stood): after a gentile who ate Paschal lambs in Jerusalem was exposed through R. Judah b. Bathyra's advice, Jerusalem sent him the message 'Peace unto you Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, as you are in Netzivin and your net is spread in Jerusalem.' Attests a Jewish sage resident in Nisibis before 70 CE; date c. 60 (undated, pre-70; c.). Presence only, no count.
